strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP compression problem: choosing an effective teacher for a constrained student. Experiments across GPT-2 and Pythia provide useful evidence that larger teachers can produce worse pruned students under the tested training recipe.

MiniMA is a useful practical contribution with broad English and Chinese evaluation. Table 4 reports improvements from distillation across all six benchmarks, including MMLU from 25.39 to 28.51 and GSM8K from 5.08 to 8.11. The 7B-versus-13B comparison also supports the smaller teacher in this particular setting.

The manuscript supplies substantial implementation information, including pruning equations, data mixtures, training hyperparameters, evaluation protocols, and links to code and checkpoints. The library-compatible student architecture improves practical usability.
weaknesses: The central capacity-gap interpretation is confounded by student construction. Each student is pruned from its corresponding teacher, so changing teachers also changes initialization, pruning severity, and potentially student architecture. The observed deterioration could reflect pruning damage and recovery difficulty. Comparisons holding student architecture and initialization fixed are needed to establish that teacher size itself explains the effect.

The evidence does not adequately establish the transferable rule T ≈ 2.5S. The manuscript does not explain sufficiently how matched-size optima are extracted from the discrete teacher/sparsity grid or how the precise regression coefficients are obtained. It provides no uncertainty estimates or held-out prediction assessment. Appendix B compares only 90% and 100% checkpoints of the same training trajectories, offering little evidence of invariance across data scales. Comparing 7B and 13B teachers for one large student likewise does not locate an optimum.

The compute-frontier claim requires material correction. Appendix A counts student training and teacher inference but omits the teacher adaptation in Appendix C. Using the paper's own approximation, adapting 7B parameters on 126B tokens adds approximately 5.3 × 10^21 FLOPs, increasing the reported pipeline cost from approximately 4.0 to 9.3 × 10^21 FLOPs before original teacher pretraining. Marginal and total costs should be distinguished consistently. Rumor-based estimates for competing models further weaken the frontier comparison, and one student configuration cannot establish superiority at every compute budget.

The 'impossible triangle' is presented more strongly than its support warrants. Reporting overheads for two previous methods does not establish a general impossibility result, particularly without operational definitions of good performance and small additional compute. This should be framed as a motivating resource tradeoff.

MiniChat's evaluation needs stronger reporting and more cautious interpretation. GPT-4 version, response-order controls, decoding settings, and human-rating counts are insufficiently specified, and uncertainty is absent. Appendix M incorrectly interprets Spearman correlation 0.54 as 54% consistency. Appendix K acknowledges unresolved contamination, while the supposedly successful coding example in Table 15 incorrectly returns the first array when the second is empty. These issues weaken the supplementary quality claims. The unresolved central-law validation and compute accounting are the decisive reasons for recommending revision before Findings.
